passage: On Monday Shreya, five, was quiet at the bus stop and only looked at her shoes. On Wednesday her cousin Nazia taught her a clapping rhyme about a train, and Shreya chanted "chhuk-chhuk, chhuk-chhuk" all through dinner, barking like a dog between the lines. On Saturday at the park she mooed at the slide, said "whoosh" for every swing and laughed until she got hiccups. Nazia giggled along, and neither girl seemed to be laughing at anyone.

qa.q: What rhyme did Nazia teach Shreya on Wednesday?
qa.a: A clapping rhyme about a train, which Shreya chanted as "chhuk-chhuk, chhuk-chhuk" at dinner.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling at the park on Saturday, judging by her sounds?
qa.a: Most likely joy, since she mooed, said "whoosh" and laughed until she got hiccups. She may also have been simply practising sounds she liked. 😊

qa.q: How could an adult support Shreya's sound play?
qa.a: Join in with a rhyme or an animal sound when she invites them, and enjoy it rather than hushing her.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Shreya's mooing?
qa.a: As a shared game, since Nazia giggled along and nothing suggests she felt mocked.

grounding: Shows a preschooler chanting a rhyme and imitating animals and sound effects as play with a cousin.

passage: The wedding hall was so loud that Aditi, six, had to shout her rhyme to Ishita over the band. "Tick-tock, tick-tock, the clock says stop!" Then she crowed like a rooster, honked like a car and went "boing" at every balloon. Ishita, her older sister, grinned and crowed back. An uncle nearby frowned at the noise, but Aditi kept looking at her sister, waiting for the next turn.

qa.q: Where was Aditi when she chanted her rhyme?
qa.a: In a wedding hall, where a band was playing loudly.

qa.q: Why did Aditi keep making sounds even though an uncle frowned?
qa.a: Most likely she wanted to share the fun with Ishita, shown by her waiting for her sister's next turn. Another reading is that she was simply excited by all the noise around her.

qa.q: What could a parent do if the sounds start to bother guests?
qa.a: Take the girls to a quieter corner or outside, where they can keep playing with sounds freely.

qa.q: How might the uncle see Aditi's sounds?
qa.a: As plain noise in a busy hall, since he may not realise it is play. His frown alone does not show she is doing anything hurtful.

grounding: Shows a preschooler imitating animals and sound effects for play and sharing joy, in a noisy hall.

passage: Dolma, five, woke in the dark flat when the power cut stopped the fan. She hugged her stuffed yak and sang under her breath, the same three-line lullaby, slowly. In the next room her father Anirban heard it and stood at her door without switching on the torch. "Can I sit with you?" he asked. Dolma nodded, still singing, and he hummed the tune quietly until the fan whirred back to life.

qa.q: What did Dolma hold while she sang?
qa.a: A stuffed yak.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she started singing, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Probably fear of the dark after the fan stopped, since she sang under her breath and clung to her toy. She might also have been simply restless, but the timing points to fright.

qa.q: How did Anirban respond in a helpful way?
qa.a: He asked before sitting down and hummed quietly, joining her song only after she nodded. 🤍

qa.q: What might Anirban have been thinking as he stood at the door?
qa.a: Probably that the singing was helping her cope, so he wanted to stay near without taking over. He could also have been unsure whether she wanted company.

grounding: Shows a child singing softly to herself and a toy when frightened, with a parent honouring it and joining when invited.

passage:
"Rehana, why are you whispering to Bunny?" Her mother Jyoti stood in the doorway.
"I'm not whispering. I'm singing."
"Sing louder, then, so I can hear."
"No. It's a quiet song. Bunny is scared of the thunder."
"Is Bunny scared, or are you?"
"Bunny. ...Maybe a little me."
"Can I sing too?"
"You can do the humming part."
Jyoti hummed while the thunder rolled outside, and Rehana's small voice steadied on the last line.

qa.q: Who did Rehana say was scared of the thunder?
qa.a: Bunny.

qa.q: What does Rehana's "Maybe a little me" suggest?
qa.a: She is a bit frightened herself and is using the song for comfort. She may have named Bunny first because that was easier than admitting it.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped, and why?
qa.a: She asked to join and took only the humming part Rehana offered, so the song stayed Rehana's own comfort.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel hearing "Maybe a little me"?
qa.a: Likely tender and a little concerned, and glad Rehana trusted her with it.

grounding: Shows a child singing quietly to a toy when scared, and a parent joining only when invited.

passage: I'm Sahil from the second floor, and this is what I saw. I was carrying groceries into the lift when little Dolma from the third floor stood behind her mother's leg. Her mother said, "Say namaste to Sahil uncle." Dolma peeked out, said "Ha-llo" to my shoes and hid again. Next morning she said, "My name is Dolma," clearly, then went quiet. Maybe she's shy, or maybe she was just tired. I said, "Thank you for saying hello," and left it there.

qa.q: Where did Sahil first meet Dolma in the passage?
qa.a: At the lift, where he was carrying groceries.

qa.q: Why might Dolma have hidden behind her mother's leg?
qa.a: Most likely shyness with a grown-up she barely knows. Another reading is that she was simply tired.

qa.q: How could Dolma's mother support her learning to greet?
qa.a: Keep prompting kindly and let her greet in her own time, accepting a quiet hello without pressure.

qa.q: How does Sahil seem to feel about Dolma's greeting?
qa.a: Warm and unbothered. He thanked her and left it there, so he seems to treat her small hello as enough. 🙂

grounding: Shows a preschooler learning to greet and give her name with prompting, with shyness respected, seen by a neighbour.

passage: On his first day at nursery, Pranav, five, held his father's hand and said nothing when Vidya Miss said good morning. On the fourth day she crouched and asked, "Can you tell me your name?" Pranav whispered "Pranav" and looked at the floor. On the tenth day he walked in, said, "Good morning, Miss," and when she handed him the crayon box he said, "Thank you!" loudly, then grinned at his father by the door.

qa.q: What did Pranav say when Vidya handed him the crayon box?
qa.a: "Thank you!"

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling on his first day, and what else could explain his silence?
qa.a: Probably shyness in a new place, shown by holding his father's hand and staying silent. He could also have been sleepy or just not ready to speak.

qa.q: What did Vidya do that helped Pranav?
qa.a: She crouched to his level and asked a small question without forcing a reply, giving him time until he was ready.

qa.q: How might Pranav's father have felt on the tenth day?
qa.a: Probably proud and perhaps relieved, since Pranav grinned at him after speaking up.

grounding: Shows a preschooler gradually learning to greet, give a name and say thank you, with shyness respected.

passage: Yusuf, five, went with his aunt Reena to meet her old teacher. At the door Reena said, "Namaste, ma'am," with folded hands. Yusuf copied her, then bent down and touched the teacher's feet. She laughed kindly. "Namaste is plenty, beta. In our house we just fold hands." Yusuf glanced up at Reena, unsure. Reena whispered, "That was lovely. Every family does it a little differently."

qa.q: What two things did Yusuf do to greet the teacher?
qa.a: He folded his hands and then bent down to touch her feet.

qa.q: What might Yusuf be worried about after the teacher laughed?
qa.a: Whether he had done it wrong. His glance suggests he was unsure, though he might also have been checking that she approved.

qa.q: What could Reena say later to help Yusuf feel safe about greetings?
qa.a: Tell him kindly that families greet differently and that he was being respectful, and show him the way this teacher prefers.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Yusuf's gesture?
qa.a: As a sweet sign of respect. She laughed kindly rather than correcting him sharply, even though her own custom is to fold hands. 🙂

grounding: Shows a child greeting elders with namaste and feet-touching, with customs differing and the child taught kindly.

passage:
"Rafiq, Nani is here. Go and say salaam."
"Do I touch her feet?"
"Who told you that?"
"Aarav does, at school."
"Some families do, some don't. In ours we say salaam, and a hug if Nani wants one."
"What if I forget?"
"Then Nani will smile and you say it again."
Rafiq's mother Vinita gave him a small nudge. He walked over, said, "Salaam, Nani," and waited. Nani opened her arms.

qa.q: Who does Rafiq say touches feet at school?
qa.a: Aarav.

qa.q: What was Rafiq worried about when he asked, "What if I forget?"
qa.a: Getting the greeting wrong in front of Nani. He may also simply have wanted reassurance from his mother.

qa.q: How did Vinita handle Rafiq's question kindly?
qa.a: She explained that families differ and told him forgetting is fine, instead of scolding him.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Rafiq says salaam and waits?
qa.a: Likely touched and welcoming, since she opened her arms. She might equally have been glad to see him however he greeted her.

grounding: Shows a child unsure whether to touch elders' feet or say salaam, taught kindly that customs vary.

passage: Karthik, five, ran into the village tea shop holding a paper. "Sabina Akka, see my drawing! This is a cow, this is me, the cow ran, then I ran, and before that the rain came." Sabina, who ran the shop, tilted her head. "And then what happened?" "The cow sat in the puddle. Then Amma called." "So the rain came first, then the cow ran?" "Yes!" He beamed and pointed to a blue scribble. "That is the rain."

qa.q: What did Karthik say the cow did at the end?
qa.a: The cow sat in the puddle.

qa.q: What does Karthik's beaming after Sabina's question suggest?
qa.a: That he felt proud and happy to be listened to. The mixed-up order more likely shows he is still learning to tell events in sequence than that he is unsure.

qa.q: Why does "And then what happened?" work as a prompt?
qa.a: It invites more detail and helps sort out the order without telling him he got it wrong.

qa.q: How might Sabina see Karthik's jumbled story?
qa.a: As a normal, charming attempt by a small child. She tilts her head and asks gently instead of correcting him. 🙂

grounding: Shows a preschooler describing a drawing with gaps and mixed-up order, helped by a patient prompt.

passage: After the playground in Rotterdam, Elif, six, told her grandmother Vera, "Me and Noor went on the big slide, and then the ball came, and I fell down, and the ball was yellow." Vera knelt. "Take your time. What happened first?" "We went on the slide. Then the ball came. Then I fell. It didn't hurt much." Vera nodded. "Thank you for telling me all of it." Elif skipped ahead, swinging her hand.

qa.q: What colour was the ball in Elif's report?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: How does Elif seem to feel about the fall?
qa.a: Fairly unbothered, since she says it didn't hurt much and skips off. She may have been a little shaken and simply moved on to something else.

qa.q: What could Vera do to get a clearer picture of what happened?
qa.a: Keep asking calm prompts like "What happened first?" and let Elif tell it in her own way, without saying she is wrong.

qa.q: How might Vera feel while listening?
qa.a: Attentive and patient, and perhaps a little concerned about the fall until Elif says it didn't hurt much.

grounding: Shows a preschooler reporting what happened at play with gaps, helped by patient prompts.

passage: Diego, five, told his babysitter Ulla that a dragon had visited kindergarten and eaten all the sandwiches. "It was green, bigger than the school, and it breathed on Mateo's hat." Ulla smiled. "Wow. Was it a pretend dragon or a real one?" Diego thought. "Pretend. Mateo was the dragon." "And who really ate the sandwiches?" "We did. At snack." He grinned and roared quietly at the sofa.

qa.q: What did Diego say the dragon breathed on?
qa.a: Mateo's hat.

qa.q: What was Diego feeling as he told the dragon story?
qa.a: Excited and playful, shown by the details and his grin. He was not necessarily trying to fool anyone, since he happily said Mateo was the dragon.

qa.q: How did Ulla help separate pretend from real?
qa.a: She played along first, then asked a friendly question about pretend or real, without calling him a liar.

qa.q: How might Ulla see Diego's dragon tale?
qa.a: As imaginative play. She smiles and stays curious, so she does not treat it as lying. 😊

grounding: Shows a child mixing fantasy and fact in a story, with an adult gently separating pretend from real.

passage: Chandrika Ma'am noticed a puddle on the floor beside the class fish tank. Sachin, six, said, "A shark jumped out and splashed everything, and I saved the fish with my cape." Chandrika crouched. "A shark sounds exciting. I need to know what really happened, because the floor is slippery." Sachin looked at his shoes. "I was carrying the fish's water cup. It tipped." "Thank you for telling me. Let's get the mop together."

qa.q: What did Sachin say jumped out of the tank at first?
qa.a: A shark.

qa.q: What might Sachin have been feeling when he looked at his shoes?
qa.a: Probably embarrassment or worry about being in trouble. He could also have been thinking about what to say next.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika's approach work?
qa.a: She acknowledged the story warmly before asking for the facts, gave a reason, and then invited him to help, so he could tell the truth without feeling labelled.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have seen the shark story at first?
qa.a: As a child's imaginative cover for a small accident, not a serious lie. She still needed the real facts because the wet floor was slippery.

grounding: Shows a child narrating with fantasy where facts matter, and a teacher gently separating pretend from real.

passage: Yogesh here, I drive the school van. This morning the teacher told the children to leave their bags at the door, and Dhruv, five, stood frozen. His ears went red. Then he tugged her sleeve. "Miss, I didn't understand. Say it again?" She repeated it slowly and smiled. "Good asking, Dhruv." He nodded and went in. The boy beside him pretended he'd got it and dropped his bag in the wrong spot. I can't say who was more nervous.

qa.q: What is Yogesh's job at the school?
qa.a: He drives the school van.

qa.q: What might Dhruv have felt before he asked the teacher?
qa.a: Some nervousness, hinted by standing frozen with red ears. He could also have been concentrating. He asked anyway.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that made asking easier?
qa.a: She repeated the instruction slowly and praised the asking, so not knowing did not feel shameful.

qa.q: How might the boy who pretended he had understood feel later?
qa.a: Possibly worried or embarrassed once he notices his bag is in the wrong spot, though we cannot be sure what he was thinking.

grounding: Shows a young child saying he did not understand and asking for it again, praised by the teacher, seen by a van driver.

passage: On Monday Parul, six, nodded when her father Harish said, "Put the clothes in the blue box." She put them in the red bag and said nothing. On Wednesday he asked again, and she said quietly, "Papa, which box?" Harish smiled. "Good question. The blue one under the bed." On Saturday at the shop he asked, "Small or big?" Parul said, "I don't understand small. Show me?" He held up both. She pointed, proud.

qa.q: Which box did Harish want the clothes in?
qa.a: The blue one under the bed.

qa.q: What was Parul likely feeling on Monday when she nodded and then used the red bag?
qa.a: Probably unsure and perhaps embarrassed to say so. She may also have been distracted.

qa.q: How can Harish keep encouraging Parul to ask questions?
qa.a: Keep praising the asking, answer patiently, and show things when words are unclear.

qa.q: How might Parul feel by Saturday about not knowing something?
qa.a: Much more comfortable, since asking got a kind answer and she pointed proudly.

grounding: Shows a child moving from guessing to saying she does not understand, encouraged by a parent.

passage: Note from Maria, nursery teacher. Simran (5) asked "why" through story time, snack and the walk to the door. Why is the door red? Why is the door a door? By the sixth why she was looking at me, not the door, and smiled at each answer. I asked, "What do you think?" She said, "Maybe painters like red." By afternoon my voice was tired, but I liked her questions. Tomorrow: short answers, and a small helper job for her. 🙂

qa.q: What did Simran guess about why the door is red?
qa.a: That painters like red.

qa.q: What might Simran want, going by how she looked at Maria and smiled?
qa.a: Likely attention and connection as well as answers. Another reading is simple curiosity about the door.

qa.q: What did Maria plan to do next?
qa.a: Give short answers and a small helper job for Simran.

qa.q: How might Maria be feeling by the end of the day?
qa.a: Somewhat tired but fond of the questions, since her voice was tired yet she still liked them.

grounding: Shows a preschooler's repeated why questions carrying curiosity and a wish for attention, met with short answers and a question back.

passage: Walking home from the field, Parul, five, kept pace with her mother Vasudha. "Why is the sun red?" "Because it's evening." "Why is it evening?" "Because the day is finished." "Why?" Vasudha's feet were aching, and she laughed. "What do you think, Parul?" Parul frowned. "Maybe the sun is tired like you." "Maybe! Shall we see if it comes back tomorrow?" Parul skipped ahead, pleased.

qa.q: What did Parul guess about the sun?
qa.a: That it is tired like her mother.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha ask, "What do you think, Parul?"
qa.a: Her feet ached and she was tired, and she wanted to keep the talk going without answering forever. She may also have been curious about Parul's idea.

qa.q: What else could Vasudha try if the whys keep coming?
qa.a: Give short honest answers, ask what Parul thinks, or suggest watching for the sunrise together.

qa.q: How might Parul feel when her guess is accepted with "Maybe!"?
qa.a: Pleased and heard, as shown by skipping ahead. She may also enjoy having her mother's attention.

grounding: Shows a preschooler's repeated why questions and a parent keeping the dialogue alive by asking what the child thinks.

subtype: Certainty and I do not know [Expressing]
passage: On Sunday Chetan, five, told his grandmother Leela that the moon follows their car because it likes him. He was completely sure. On Wednesday he said flatly, "Bats are birds." Leela said, "Hm, I don't know. Let's look in the picture book." On Friday at the well she asked how deep it was. Chetan began, "Very..." then paused. "I don't know, Ajji. Can we find out?" Leela smiled and dropped a pebble in, and they listened together.

qa.q: What did Chetan say about the moon on Sunday?
qa.a: That it follows their car because it likes him.

qa.q: What does Chetan's pause on Friday suggest?
qa.a: He may be starting to notice the limits of what he knows. It could also just be caution about the well.

qa.q: How did Leela model uncertainty?
qa.a: She said "I don't know" herself and suggested finding out together in a picture book.

qa.q: How might Leela see Chetan's certain statements?
qa.a: As normal for his age. She does not scold him but shows another way of answering.

grounding: Shows a child stating things with certainty and later saying he does not know, with an adult modelling uncertainty.

subtype: Certainty and I do not know [Expressing]
passage: The bus was due in four minutes, and Manjula was hunting for her keys while Shreya, four, insisted, "The bus never comes late. It comes now." "It's often late, beta." "No, it comes now. I know." The bus didn't come. Manjula, breathless, said, "I don't know when it will come. Let's watch the road together." Shreya squinted down the lane. "I don't know either," she said, and took her mother's hand.

qa.q: What did Shreya insist about the bus?
qa.a: That it never comes late and comes now.

qa.q: What might Shreya feel when the bus did not come?
qa.a: Perhaps unsettled that her certainty was wrong, and looking for comfort. She may also simply have wanted to hold hands while waiting.

qa.q: What could Manjula say later about not knowing?
qa.a: That not knowing is fine and that they can find out together next time.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel while hunting for keys and hearing Shreya's certainty?
qa.a: Rushed and slightly stressed by the time pressure, which shows in her breathless answer, though she stays gentle.

grounding: Shows a child stating certainty about the bus, then an adult modelling I do not know under time pressure.

passage: Siddiq, five, sat on the kitchen step while his grandfather Thabo said, "Mrs Dlamini's hen laid a big egg this morning." "Really?" Siddiq's eyes went wide. "No way!" On the walk over he stretched his arms out. "It will be huge, bigger than a football!" In the coop lay an egg, large for an egg but ordinary. "It's big for an egg," said Thabo. "A football was what you hoped for." "Oh," said Siddiq. Then he held it. "It's still warm."

qa.q: Whose hen laid the egg?
qa.a: Mrs Dlamini's.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling on the walk, and what does his "Oh" at the coop suggest?
qa.a: Excited expectation, shown by wide eyes and stretched arms. The "Oh" suggests a flicker of disappointment, though the warm egg still delighted him.

qa.q: How did Thabo separate hope from fact?
qa.a: He named what was real, that it was big for an egg, and what Siddiq had hoped for, without mocking him.

qa.q: What is it like for Thabo when Siddiq's hope meets the ordinary egg?
qa.a: He probably feels a little sorry to disappoint him but wants to be honest. Siddiq holding the warm egg would reassure him.

grounding: Shows a child voicing disbelief and a big expectation, with an adult gently separating hoped from known.

passage: At circle time Nirmala Miss told the class that a new library corner would arrive on Friday. Tenzin, six, opened his eyes wide. "Really? No way!" "Yes, really." "It will be as big as the whole school," he said, spreading his arms. Nirmala smiled. "We'll see on Friday. I know there will be shelves and cushions. I don't know the size yet." Tenzin nodded and whispered to his friend, "Shelves and cushions. Maybe big."

qa.q: On what day will the new library corner arrive?
qa.a: Friday.

qa.q: How was Tenzin feeling about the news?
qa.a: Excited and hopeful, shown by wide eyes and spread arms. His "No way" could also have been a way of checking the news was real.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do to separate hope from what is known?
qa.a: She told him what she knew, shelves and cushions, and admitted what she did not, the size, without squashing his excitement.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's friend take his "Maybe big"?
qa.a: Probably as shared excitement, since it is a hopeful guess rather than a claim. The friend may join in.

grounding: Shows a child voicing disbelief and expectation, with a teacher separating what is hoped from what is known.
